Let $I$ denote the integration operator,
$$
(If)(x) = \int_0^x f(t) \, dt.
$$
Applying $I$ twice, three times, or $n$ times makes sense for every positive integer $n$. Does it make sense to apply $I$ half a time?

## Cauchy's formula for repeated integration

Integrating $n$ times collapses into a single integral:
$$
(I^n f)(x) = \frac{1}{(n-1)!} \int_0^x (x - t)^{n-1} f(t) \, dt.
$$
This follows by induction, swapping the order of integration at each step.

## Replacing the factorial

The only place where $n$ needs to be an integer is the factorial. Replacing $(n-1)!$ with $\Gamma(n)$ gives the **Riemann–Liouville fractional integral**, defined for every $\alpha > 0$:
$$
(I^\alpha f)(x) = \frac{1}{\Gamma(\alpha)} \int_0^x (x - t)^{\alpha-1} f(t) \, dt.
$$

These operators satisfy the semigroup law $I^\alpha I^\beta = I^{\alpha + \beta}$, which is a restatement of the Beta integral. In particular, $I^{1/2}$ applied twice is $I$.

## An example

For $f(x) = x^k$,
$$
I^\alpha x^k = \frac{\Gamma(k+1)}{\Gamma(k + \alpha + 1)} \, x^{k + \alpha}.
$$
Taking $k = 0$ and $\alpha = 1/2$, the half-integral of the constant function $1$ is $2\sqrt{x/\pi}$.
